newsitem.title: GERMANY: Serbs to face genocide charges in German courts.
newsitem.headline: Serbs to face genocide charges in German courts.

text.p: Two Bosnian Serbs will go on trial in Germany at the end of February, accused of taking part in the murder and torture of Moslems during the Bosnian war, the Federal Prosecutor's Office said on Wednesday.
A 33-year-old Bosnian Serb, identified only as Novislav D., and Nicola Jorgic, 50, will stand trial on the war crimes charges in Munich and Duesseldorf respectively.
"These will be the first ever war crimes trials of Bosnian Serbs in Germany," said Eva Schuebel, spokeswoman for the prosecutor's office in Karlsruhe.
Jorgic was detained in Duesseldorf in December 1995. Germany asked the United Nations war crimes tribunal in The Hague to take the case on, but the tribunal handed it back citing a heavy workload.
"The Hague wants to concentrate on the most important indicted war criminals, such as (former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan) Karadzic," Schuebel said.
Prosecutors say Jorgic led a group of Serb fighters, responsible for killing about two dozen Moslems in 1992 in the region around the northern Bosnian town of Doboj, now controlled by Serbs.

He was charged last October with genocide in 14 cases, in combination with murder, causing grievous bodily harm, unlawful detention and blackmail with intent to rob. He denies the charges and says he is a victim of mistaken identity.

Novislav D., who has lived in Germany since 1993, is charged with complicity in genocide and murder. He is believed to have been one of a group of Serb fighters responsible for carrying out ethnic cleansing in Bosnia's Foca region.
The prosecutor's office says he took part in a raid in June 1992 in which 14 Moslem men were killed and 15 others taken prisoner. Those 15 were never seen again.
Novislav D., whose surname authorities declined to provide, was arrested in Munich on January 16, 1996.

Although the alleged offences were not committed in Germany, the men can be tried here under a passage of international law which says the perpetrators of genocide may not receive shelter anywhere and can be tried abroad.
Federal prosecutors are investigating 48 other people suspected of war crimes in former Yugoslavia, and have issued arrest warrants for five believed to be living in Germany.
